summary: Defines how the X.500 Directory can be used to support routing in the Message Handling System, mapping an O/R address to the next message transfer agent that is nearer the destination. It is an experimental protocol.

eli5.summary: A mail carrier needs to know which post office is next on the way to a house. This memo uses a big directory to look that up.

questions: how does x.500 support x.400 routing
what is a routing tree in x.400
subtitle: Using the X.500 Directory as a global routing table so X.400 mail servers can find the next hop toward a recipient.

tldr.problem: Setting up routing for X.400 message handling systems was a black art of gathering tables and editing complex configuration files, and it did not scale to the global network the authors had in mind.
tldr.mechanism: The memo stores routing information in the X.500 Directory as routing trees that follow the O/R Address hierarchy. An MTA looks up a recipient's O/R Address in an ordered list of trees to find a suitable next-hop MTA.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1801 is an Experimental specification. It describes the longer-term approach and says that security issues are not discussed in the memo.

today: RFC 1801 is an Experimental specification and is not listed as obsoleted or updated by any other RFC. It describes the longer-term, Directory-based approach to X.400 routing that the author envisaged in 1995.

sections.title: The Routing Problem and Its Goals
sections.content:
MHS routing is the problem of controlling the path of a message as it crosses one or more Message Transfer Agents (MTAs) to reach its recipients. It starts with a recipient O/R Address and the parameters of the message. The key step is to map the address onto an MTA, the next hop, that is in some sense nearer to the destination user agent. This is repeated until the message can be delivered directly to the recipient.

The memo sets many goals. Routing should be straightforward to manage, because configuring routing for current systems is described as a black art and the most serious headache for most mail system managers. It should also be economical, robust, able to cope with link failures and load sharing, dynamic and automatic, and robust against bad policy. It should deal with X.400 and RFC 822 and their interaction, and be global in scope, at a scale of the order of 1,000,000 to 100,000,000 MTAs and organisations. Dynamic load balancing and advanced optimisation for messages with many recipients are not initial goals.

This document specifies the envisaged longer-term approach. It contrasts with an interim table-based approach, whose format is defined in RFC 1465.
sections.eli5: Getting a letter across the world takes many stops. The goal is a simple, shared way for each stop to know the next stop, without anyone keeping huge hand-made lists.

sections.title: Direct and Indirect Connection, and Communities
sections.content:
Routing can range from high connectivity, where all MTAs are fully interconnected like the Domain Name System on the Internet, to low connectivity like the UUCP network. The memo argues for an intermediate approach, supporting both direct and indirect connectivity. Relaying costs extra hops and delay, but it is useful for charge optimisation, copy optimisation, format conversion, distribution list expansion, hiding the internal structure of an organisation behind a single entry point, and applying a uniform access policy.

To organise this, the memo uses communities. A community is a scope in which an MTA advertises its services and learns about others. The types are:

  • the open community, with public, global scope;
  • the local community, private to one MTA;
  • hierarchical communities, which are subtrees of the O/R Address tree and allow firewalls;
  • closed communities, sets of MTAs that agree to route among themselves.

Agreements between MTAs are either bilateral, between a pair, or open, among a collection acting cooperatively.
sections.eli5: Some mail goes straight to the door, and some goes through a big sorting office first. There are public sorting offices anyone can use, and private ones only certain people can use.

sections.title: Routing Trees in the Directory
sections.content:
Each community is represented in the X.500 Directory as a routing tree whose names follow the O/R Address hierarchy. The open community routing tree starts at the root of the Directory Information Tree (DIT) and also instantiates the global O/R Address space. Other routing trees are rooted at an entry of object class routingTreeRoot, placed at an arbitrary point in the DIT. For example, the O/R Address P=ABC; A=XYZMail; C=GB has the distinguished name PRMD=ABC, ADMD=XYZMail, C=GB in the open tree. A private tree could be rooted at CN=Zydeco Routing Tree, O=Zydeco Services, C=GB.

To look up an address, map it onto the O/R Address hierarchy to get a distinguished name, append that to the name of the routing tree, and look up the whole name. The root of a non-open tree can hold default routing information, and a tree can contain aliases into other trees. Every non-skeletal node carries the auxiliary object class routingInformation. It can hold these attributes, among others:

  • mTAInfo: the list of next-hop MTAs, which is the key information for a node;
  • routingFilter: routing on the part of the address not yet matched, such as a substring match;
  • subtreeInformation: whether the node is authoritative for the level below, which allows invalid addresses to be rejected;
  • routingFailureAction: what to do when no MTA at the node can be used;
  • accessMD: indirect access through another management domain.
sections.eli5: The phone book is arranged just like addresses: country, then company, then person. To find the next stop you look up the address in the book, and a node can say 'send it to this post office'.

sections.title: Choosing a Route
sections.content:
An MTA's list of routing trees, and the order to use them, is held in the routingTreeList attribute. A common order is to try shared private trees first, then the open tree, then fall back to a default route from one of the private trees. Within one tree the algorithm finds the longest match for the address and then considers each parent in turn.

When a matched node cannot be used directly, routingFailureAction says what happens next (see the table below). The mTAInfo attribute lists MTAs with a route weight, an integer from 0 to 20 where lower is better. Three reference points are given: 0 for an MTA that can deliver directly to the whole subtree, 5 for a preferred MTA and 10 for a backup. With equal weights the choice is random, which helps load balancing. Weights from different subtrees cannot generally be compared.

Routing filters are checked before the mTAInfo and accessMD attributes. In the memo's example, an entry has two filters on the x121 attribute: one with no regular expression for a default fax gateway, and one with the expression ^9262 and a lower weight to send German faxes to a gateway in Germany.

Lookups are made with Directory read operations, and the memo maps Directory errors onto four outcomes: entry found, entry not found, temporary reject and permanent reject. A referral is followed.
sections.eli5: If one post office is closed, the book says where to try next. Each choice has a score, and the lowest score is the best choice. If two are tied, you pick one by chance.

sections.title: The Overall Routing Algorithm
sections.content:
The routing algorithm follows the sequence of routing trees. As nodes are matched, they yield a set of candidate MTAs. If all of them are rejected, the trees are followed further. A candidate MTA is evaluated against these criteria:

  • If it is the local MTA, deliver locally.
  • It must support a protocol the current MTA supports. This can be an RFC 822 protocol as well as an X.400 protocol.
  • The protocols must share a common transport community.
  • It must have no capability restrictions and no policy restrictions that prevent transfer of the message.
  • The current MTA must meet its authentication requirements, and if a bilateral agreement applies, the MTA must be in the local set of bilateral agreements.
  • Where the recipient's capabilities can be determined, there should be no mismatch, or reformatting must be possible.

Other sections cover MTA names and attributes, bilateral agreements, pulling messages, authentication, policy, redirects, non-delivery information and bad addresses. For performance, only the Directory read function is used, and routing trees can be configured so that a decision needs only two reads.
sections.eli5: Before handing the letter to the next post office, the carrier checks that it speaks the same language, accepts this kind of letter and will let the carrier in.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The Security Considerations section of this memo states only that security issues are not discussed in this memo. Security-related matters appear earlier as part of the routing design, for example authentication requirements on MTAs and bilateral agreements, but the memo does not provide a separate security analysis.
sections.eli5: The memo does not have a chapter about keeping the mail safe, although it does talk about checking who is allowed to connect.

viz.caption: OPEN COMMUNITY ROUTING TREE ENTRY FOR PRMD=ABC (RFC 1801 EXAMPLE)

items.label: next-level
items.desc: Move up a level in the current tree. This is the default if the attribute is omitted.

items.label: next-tree-only
items.desc: Move to the next tree and do no further processing on this one.

items.label: next-tree-first
items.desc: Move to the next tree, then come back to the next level of this one when done.

items.label: stop
items.desc: The address is unroutable. No further processing in any tree.
